You've said in the report, you've said in your witness statements here that the larger town centres were not damaged to any great extent, and your theory in the report was so that people could settle in them. You also say that the burning frustrated the Croatian government's return plans for displaced persons. Now, given that the burning, according to you, occurred in the outlying areas, I return to you my original question which is: Is it your position that the burning in the outlying areas was planned by the Croatian government which frustrated the Croatian government's plan to return displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that what we observed in the countryside suggested very much a plan. What we observed in the larger town centres also suggested a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did the burning obstruct the Croatian government's plan to return displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The burning of the part of the countryside, I think, frustrated the population that had lived in the countryside to come back. One can speculate, even today, if the countryside people should live in the towns. It became an issue as the winter set in, that in fact the destruction had been too much so that it was difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are moving away from an answer to the question. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it simple enough to say, Mr. Liborius, that you cannot reconcile those two positions that you have. Isn't that the right answer? I have given you five opportunities, I'll give you another one if you wish. But isn't the truth that you can't reconcile those two positions?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question I don't answer -- understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the witness has come. We have seen what he wrote on paper, we have heard his testimony, and whether he is able to reconcile the two is -- you have pointed to him that, in your view, apparently, that there are plans that would -- not reconcilable, that's clearly implied in your questions, the witness whether he can reconcile it, I don't know whether that's of major importance. We give him -- can you reconcile the two plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you see a countryside being destroyed -- I'm trying to reconcile, you see a countryside being destroyed, you don't want people there. You want to have them in the larger towns where they're easier to control. You don't want a section of the population to return that used to live in the countryside, some in the cities as well, then it makes sense. Later on, when it dawns upon people that the destruction has been too much, then a problem kicks in. And that was a mood that I felt and still do feel when I discuss with colleagues and friends from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who are the colleagues and friends from the area that you have discussions with?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of my former monitoring colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And who are the friends from the area?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer that question? Does it give any added value to my findings in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If can you answer the question, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a few friends, Croats, Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say "friends," and if you are asked who they are, then there is no need to say that you have friends because that's what you said already, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness wants to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that is an another matter. If you are hesitant to give their names in public, then you can ask for private session, but -- so either in private session or in public session, please tell us who the friends are you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I prefer a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, D743, please. And now I would like page 1D50-0238, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm taking you back to the entry for the 19th of August, Mr. Liborius, in your notebook. We discussed this yesterday. This is that report to the Danish delegation. My question for you, sir, is the report on the 26th, is that the report that you also submitted to the Danish delegation and the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you mean the identical or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's identical or not, sir. Is that substantively the same report as you submitted to the DAN DEL, or the Danish delegation?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I don't have the reports at hand, I don't know the precise answer. However, there would be different subjects covered. But I really can't tell you because I don't have the reports at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The notation there on the bottom under CRO about the burning being ethnic cleansing. Do you see that? You then after this entry went out on patrols on the 21st, 22nd, 23rd, 24th, and 25th, is it fair to say that you had reached your conclusion about ethnic cleansing before you went out on those patrols?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't make prior conclusions. If you see in the notebook, you will see a parenthesis around the word [Foreign language spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which means what?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What do the parenthesis mean?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it is something that should be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, tell me what you believe -- when I say anarchy, what does anarchy mean to you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anarchy can be a state of -- a situation where this is a lack of order. It can be a free-for-all situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The dictionary definition of it is: Political and social disorder due to the absence of governmental control. Is that your understanding -- you do you accept that as a definition of the word "anarchy"?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is many pseudonyms to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But basically that's what you've always understood anarchy to mean, right, is absence of governmental control?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anarchy is a fairly broad term, also, to me. It can also be, as I said, a free-for-all situation. I recall that used the anarchy sometimes in reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree with me that the destruction after the 4th of August, when it began, it was an anarchial [sic] destruction?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does ring a bell somewhere in the reporting, I think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness actually says in his report -- I think it might be fair to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The witness, Mr. Misetic, has given an answer on what anarchy could mean. Well, now, I could bore you a day with explanations on lines of thought which consider individuals to be not bound by -- I mean, this is a rather -- this is a concept which -- what I'd like to know - and apparently what you would like to know- is not what -- if you are talking about anarchy in those circumstances, what do you refer to at that moment, rather than to ask the witness whether something in the dictionary is -- I could give you -- yes, I know that. At the same time, we could give him ten dictionaries and descriptions and a philosophical ones, et cetera, and then to ask him to choose; that is, of course, the same problem as the photo spread, isn't it? If you get one photograph, you would say yes or no, whereas it really gets a meaning if you give more. Now, I'm not seeking to put to the witness 15 different -- different descriptions of what anarchy is. What I would like to know, if he uses that word, what he means. That's what is -- is all about and not to be introduced by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what -- my objective, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- but sometimes in cross-examination there are reasons that we do things the way we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, and it may be clear to you that this might not be the most effective way in getting to what the Chamber needs, and I think the purpose is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I hope that in the next 20 minutes you will see that I had a method to my madness, as they say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I also, for the record, believe the objection was improper. But let's turn to P824, please. If we could go seven pages in on this document, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So this is your 100-day report. And in the summary, this is the first page of text, the second sentence: "In general the period began with total anarchial destruction by looting and burning of the countryside and looting of the town centres." If we could go now to page 20 of this document, please. It is actually page 17 written but it is the 20th page in the electronic version. There we go. Now, sir, I want you to look at that entry. In the Varivode, you're talking about Varivode, and three sentences in you're talking on September 28, is where we start, and then it says: "In the whole eight weeks, before the situation was one of even more anarchy than today." And I note four different occasions in your report you refer to anarchial destruction, anarchy on page 17. On page 26 you write "lack of determination to establish working judicial systems is one of the factors contributing to the anarchy." And then page 29 you again refer to the consequences of this general anarchy. Anarchy is the absence of governmental control. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you can ask the witness what he meant by anarchy here and not be given a definition and say, Is this the definition, and then to draw your own conclusions. What did you mean when you use the word "anarchy" in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant that the absence of what I would call a normal law and order, normality in society, lack of looting and burning in a society where you would be able to -- to say, Okay this is normal. Anarchy was as opposed to unnormal. In the context of the report, in the two examples Mr. Misetic is referring to, what I meant was the breakdown of this normality. I do understand that you can discuss the word or the semantics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need to enter into a debate in what you could discuss about anarchy. You've answered my question. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say in the same report, if we can go back down to page 4 of the document -- actually, sorry, page 7, which is numbered page 4 in the document. Again, at the bottom of the first paragraph: "Largely due to this wanton self-inflicted destruction, the ambitious Croatian plan for the return of large numbers of displaced persons from 1991 proved impossible by the onset of winter." Tell us why the destruction made the Croatian plan impossible for the return of displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lack of property. Inhabitable probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You go on to say: "Those Serbs and Croats who stayed in the area during the Krajina time soon faced problems; ongoing looting, threats, and random human rights violations and discrimination." Tell us more about the human rights violations against Croats in the sector during the first 100 days after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you an example. In some of the mixed marriages - one Croat, one Serb - where they had been brave enough to stay during the RSK years, sometimes their houses were looted. Sometimes their property was stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: According to what we just went through, in the first portion of today's session you also seem to conclude that the homes and villages of Croatians, according to the 1991 census, were also burned down. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi has an objection against the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's -- assumes facts not in evidence. What the witness said, he observed -- and he said it about four times. He observed burning on the ground irrespective of Serb or Croatian population, and then it was put to him that whether -- he didn't know whether in 1991 these were inhabited by Croats or Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, first of all, assumption of facts which are not in evidence is one of the -- I would say one of the features of a leading question, and leading questions are within certain limits allowed within cross-examination; that's one. If you say Mr. Misetic misrepresented the evidence of the witness he did put to him, then, the question says, You also seem to include, that is a conclusion or a professional conclusion drawn by Mr. Misetic and not necessarily a misrepresentation of what the witness said. At the same time, to include that, Mr. Misetic, might not lead to clear and unequivocal answers. You're invited to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, your findings were that even Croatian villages had been burned down after Operation Storm. Isn't that correct? Croatian-majority villages, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My findings were that villages I observed being burned down was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you had no -- even as of November 1995 you never followed up to see if the villages that you had described as being burned, you never followed up to check the ethnic composition of those villages. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have, a couple of times, indicated how we worked, what was the object of observation. A village, burned or not burned. The discussions we took in the longer reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to cut this short. Would you agree that, at least that's how I understood your evidence, that you did not exclude for the possibility that villages that were, by majority, Croat in 1991, and of which you kept the possibility open, that the composition of the population may have changed since then, were also destroyed during or after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page ten of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "The plan of returning several tens of thousands in the first month was therefore impossible. Instead, many DPs still occupy the hotels and accommodations causing big frustration for the Croats living in those holding areas in the former free Croatia." Tell us a little bit more about how the inability of to return DPs caused frustration for Croats living in the holding areas in the former free Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frustrations experienced by the displaced persons were, among others, congestion in their facilities, lack of normal life for their families, lack of opportunities to resume their normal work, lack of many of the aspects that would be associated with life in their former areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think that when you talked to displaced persons living in collective centres, that the feelings they expressed, that their wishes they had, as they could not be fulfilled, it caused frustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What the report actually says, sir -- and we can turn the page back. Page 6 of this document. There we go. The caption is housing problems and looting. You then list a series of incidents of looting. Then you turn the page. Now, in your report, as a result of all of these problems of criminality, you write: "The plan of returning several tens of thousands in the first month was therefore impossible." What I'm asking you is: Why did the illegality make the return of tens of thousands impossible?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would see the situation, much of the property was in -- the state the property was in, lacking roofs, lacking doors, lacking everything that is associated with a normal habitable accommodation, house, apartment, then it would be pretty clear that moving larger numbers of population, would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think we agree on that, sir. I just want to be clear. What you're say something that the burning and looting that took place after Operation Storm frustrated the return of several tens of thousands of displaced persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in addition to that, you write that the fact that the displaced persons couldn't get back frustrated the people that lived in, what you refer to as former free Croatia, because the displaced persons were still living in the hotels and accommodations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- quite complex. There were persons living in accommodation centres. There were persons living with different family members. There were even Bosnian Croats, and that is what you are also highlighting in this particular section of the report. So the picture was not very simple. It was a mixed picture. But common for all of these persons was that the -- that the -- the material basis was insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to get back to my question, you're aware that hotels along the Croatian coast, for example, during the war were used to house displaced persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Those hotels could not return to their function as hotels because the displaced persons were still living in them as a result of their inability to return to their homes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that's what you mean when you say that the burning and looting frustrated the Croats living in the holding areas in the former free Croatia. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a large element in it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with a problem that the displaced persons were having into September of 1995 receiving any government assistance in the form of funds from the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am familiar with a problem that they had in receiving the government assistance, well, again, off the top of my head, I remembered that some people complained that sometimes their monthly allowance or - I lack the proper English word - the support came later or it was to be shared with more people or that stuff, that sort of ... Could you be more specific as to what sort of problems -- or what sort of problem, please. I, in my 100-day report, also discuss a host of problems experienced by people as I had observed it, talked to them. I wonder if you could point to some of the specific ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked whether the witness was aware of a problem where he says that he sees perhaps many problems. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll call up 65 ter 1567, please. And if we could go to page 3 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see it is a RC Knin report.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have the start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not okay. Could I please have time to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a specific portion of this on page 3 that I'd like to draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, if you read the heading, and if you would then follow Mr. Misetic to page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and if the matter he raises would still require you to read the whole of the document, please tell us then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, subsection d. It says: "The returning DPs are not eager to fulfil the schedule of the CR government as the infrastructure for a new life is still not existing and in many parts of the country, security cannot 100 per cent be guaranteed, de-mining, rebuilding, infrastructure, schools, employment opportunities are long-term projects. The fear is that many DPs will be forced to return long before the region can support them. There have been unconfirmed reports of few DPs receiving money for rebuilding but, in general, no one seems to have received any yet. We heard amount of 25.000 Deutschemarks." Now, I want to ask you about that point, Mr. Liborius. Are you familiar with the problem of displaced persons not receiving money from the Croatian government to rebuild?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that, on one or more occasion, that complaints about lack of reception of promised funds was brought to me by local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, then, that the Croatian government, at least as of the 2nd of September, had not provided financial assistance to displaced persons to assist them in rebuilding, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not qualified to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you feel not qualified -- unless Mr. Misetic wants to further explore the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next sentence says: "Official sources are convinced that a big sum will be sent by other European countries to help in re-establishing life worth situation." Are you familiar with -- who these "official sources" might be?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were generally aware that the Croatian government was seeking assistance from European countries to aid DPs in returning to their former homes and in rebuilding?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood at that time that the Croatian government was indeed seeking. I don't know details of it. The full details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that European aid and European aid programmes were suspended in the fall of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm familiar with it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to the 100-day report, P824, please. And if we could go to page 8, please -- I'm sorry -- yeah, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The GAB, and you write: "After 100 days one of the distinct results is the growing gap between the two different spheres ..." Do you see that? It's page 5 in your report. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll continue: "As the countryside is largely burned, the towns where the Croatian rule is obvious. The larger towns in Sector South: Knin, Drnis, Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, Korenica, and Udbina were spared from destruction in Operation Storm in August. Here utility services are in general working since September. Electricity and water and basis communications were established." And if we can skip down a little bit, you say: "Moving away from the main street the picture changes. Here the signs of destruction are still to be found. Piles of garbage, personal belonging from the previous owners of the houses spread around in the streets." Now, tell us a little bit about what you found in terms of the towns identified here in your report being essentially intact 100 days after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit about the towns, let's start with -- houses and apartments were, in general, connected to public utilities that, as the time progressed, basic cleaning of the cities were conducted, that more people returned -- or some newcomers -- we dealt with the Bosnian Croats in previous questions, that persons were introduced in the towns. Some of them, of course, being previous inhabitants before 1991. A few Serbs came back, numbers I discussed throughout the report, that it became, so to speak, an island of -- let's call it relative normality, relative normality, as opposed to the lack of facilities and lack of accommodation, all that stuff that was required in the countryside, to have people in greater numbers living there. The towns were, of course, also the places where Croat administration would be established and gradually expand. We have elsewhere in other reports also discussed the establishment of -- of these administrative structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can I stop you right there, sir, because that is a good point I want to talk to you about. You said the administrative structures of the -- sorry. You said: "In the towns, the towns of course were also the places where Croat administration would be established and gradually expand." Were -- did the Croat administration extend into the countryside as of the first 100 days?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police structures were among the first in our monitoring to be established in many areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, why did you say the towns were of course also the places where the Croat administration would be established and gradually expand. What was the difference between the towns and the countryside in terms of the administration?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we missing a verb? I think I know what you're hinting at. In the town centres, you would, as the autumn progressed, come across offices for handling property. You would come across postal offices. You would come across basic utility companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was missing from the countryside, in terms of administration?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The service provision, public utilities for instance, would be very, very slow in some areas. Some areas it would be a bit faster. The usual services - buses, postal - the provisions that on paper would be available - schools and so on - would be very seldom. But, of course, as the time moved on, some expansion of the above-mentioned would be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we have a break, Mr. Liborius, could I ask you -- I asked you yesterday to inquire on your availability in The Hague. Could you give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have identified, in negotiations with my government, six possibilities, of which I'm authorised to suggest one to be picked. In order of priority, they are: 10 November -- sorry, 7 November; second priority, 6 November; third priority, 20 October; fourth priority, 21st October; fifth priority, 10 November; sixth priority, 11 November. I am instructed to say that with regard to 10 November and 11 of November, that is pending other tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the -- yes. Would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please. This is a considerable consumption of time associated with these appearances, and I am instructed to say that these dates where one could be picked, I would have to return in the evening of the said date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I look at the 6th and the 7th of November, Mr. Liborius, you're saying that we can have you only for one day out of these six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please pick one of these dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if we would need two days, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to seek new instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, giving testimony is a civil duty, which is not subject to government instructions, and, of course, we're trying to -- that's the reason why I asked you when you would be available. Of course, we try to take into consideration all wishes. But, of course, the first and foremost principle that guides us is the interest of justice in performing our duties. If have you an opportunity -- yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We could provide a letter of support to the Danish government as we did, I think, at the previous occasion which I think was relatively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course the Chamber is always happy if the Prosecution supports anything the Chamber has on its mind. But -- and, again, it's appreciated. But we are not used, Mr. Liborius, that if there is, in the interests of justice, a need to hear the testimony of a witness, that we limit ourselves if we consider it important, in order to guarantee a fair trial, to limit ourselves as far as time is concerned. I hope you will understand this. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just if the Defence can submit a letter of support as well. If that will help, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that all parties support the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, we want to be helpful, no doubt about that. There are a couple of issues that I would like to discuss, and I'm not so familiar with the format here. Either we could take it outside of court or in some other sessions, some of the matters are quite private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are of a private nature, usually parties are entitled to follow all communications between a witness and a chamber, but of course not everything has to be public. We can move into private session if there's anything you would like to bring to my attention of which you would think the public should not know because it's a private matter. And if you want to refer to certain issues in a more general way, then of course I could ask the parties whether they would agree; for example, you say there is a family situation and you do not want to say whether it is the birth of your next grandchild or whether it would be the divorce which has been scheduled in two weeks from now. Then, of course, I could ask the parties whether they would agree that we just hear this in their absence. So you can go -- you can ask us to go into private session. You also can try to refer to a general situation then can seek the consent of the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we meet and talk in a private circle? Probably the Defence and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that I can't start discussing matters of which I'm not aware of yet without the consent of the parties. So therefore if you don't give me a clue - you could do that in private session - as to what the subject would be, I cannot even ask the parties to give their consent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We then move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, having used now five hours and 17 minutes how much you would still -- I'm aware. No one has to explain the -- what goes quickly and what goes less quickly with this witness. That is clear to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have quite a bit of material which I am -- in light of, quite honestly, in light of today's events considering scaling back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all -- one second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't give opportunity to Madam Registrar to announce that we are in open session again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have quite a bit of material which I'd that I be given the break to review because in light of today's events I am considering scaling back some of my need to cross-examine this particular witness. And in order to avoid a transcript of biblical proportions, I am prepared to scale back some of my cross hopefully to be finished early tomorrow, and to use the balance of my time to try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First -- would that be first session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other Defence counsel, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a substantial cross-examination of this witness because of the way he -- his evidence has been presented in statement form, viva voce form. He has been allowed to present evidence to this court of his opinion, what he viewed, and we feel it's highly necessary to get into the facts, to go into documents, and to challenge conclusions as to whether he knew what he was talking about. That takes time and I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that. I'm just asking you how much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I was an eight-hour man as well, Your Honour, and I always do my best do get through this material quickly, but the range of his evidence and the nature of it has caused me with my team to make a file that is substantial, and I will deal with it very expeditiously and try to get it down to six hours, but it is very difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not ignoring difficulties the parties are facing. That's clear. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have at a minimum two hours worth of cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking this, because, Mr. Waespi, I'm also looking at you at this moment, that tomorrow, first session for Mr. Misetic, and let's just work on the basis of the Chamber granting your requests for time, then we would have six hours at the minimum for Mr. Kay which would take us tomorrow through the whole of the day. Then we'd still have the Markac Defence. Mr. Waespi, from my experience and how I see matters at this moment, I think we might not finish in one day after we have tomorrow concluded. Tomorrow, we'll have to conclude at 6.00. It is -- we checked the reasonable requirements for the travelling of the witness, which would mean that we would have to reserve another two days. Now, the witness gave us a few days. Of course, it's always best to have them as close to the testimony. That would be 20th and 21st of October, being third and fourth in priority. Let me just look for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just checking whether we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's the week where we will not be sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just checking that as a matter of fact, which of course is not -- yes. That's exactly the week in which we decided not sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a good suggestion or not. It's pretty obvious that we will not finish with this witness tomorrow. My suggestion would be rather than going the full day to have the normal morning sitting, since we're not going to finish, allow him to get home earlier, and then perhaps finish him in the two days that he has available in November. That is just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With this witness, Mr. Kuzmanovic, I'm not quite confident that we would achieve that, and therefore the witness is here and has complained about the time it takes him to testify. We know one thing for sure, that tomorrow in the afternoon the Danish government will not lose more time than it loses already. So therefore, your suggestion is on the record, I'll discuss it with my colleagues, but I personally have some hesitations as the Presiding Judge who is more or less in charge of the scheduling. Mr. Waespi, since the 20th and the 21st of October are non-sitting days, and I'm hesitant to have this all re-scheduled, also in view of the fact that the witness gave as his first and second priority the 7th of November and the 6th of November, I would like you to thoroughly discuss with the witness and explain to him also his legal position, because I don't know whether his view and the professional legal opinion of the Danish government is fully in line with the views of this Chamber on duties to cooperate. And I'm trying not to seek any further problems in that respect, but if you could perhaps assist the Chamber in seeing whether the witness would be available on the 6th and the 7th of November, that -- and then I have to check whether -- I don't know that, as a matter of fact, we have already our November schedule. Let me just have a look. As far as I'm concerned there might be a risk that we could not sit in full on the 7th, but -- could you try to further discuss it and, again, the two days, I think is really what we need. And if there are any private matters which are of such urgency, please reassure the witness that the Chamber would always consider that. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, were you in a position to write down the names so as a provide them to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did have a little time for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have it on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need to go my private session. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Liborius, another matter about when to stop tomorrow -- it can be given to Mr. Misetic. We have consulted with the Victims and Witness Unit who have quite some experience with travelling times in the Netherlands, and they think that if you leave here at 6.00 that that would do. I add to that, that on the basis of 40 years of experience, I can promise you that if you leave at 5.00 that you get a traffic jam between 5.00 and 6.00, and then on from 6.00 you will be able to go to the airport. If the traffic jam at 5.00 is such that will not make it, then it makes no difference whether you leave at 5.00 or 6.00, but under normal circumstances that certainly would do if you are prepared to leave immediately of after the court session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your vast experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, going back it your 100-day report there is a conclusion which says: "The lack of determination to establish working judiciary systems is one of the factors contributing to the anarchy?" And you like invite you to explain to us what the problems were with the judiciary systems?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have the page made available, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: P824, please. And then if we go to page 27 of this document, please, in English. And two more pages forward, please. One more page back, sorry, page 26. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Conclusions on part one. Under criminal acts, you say: "The lack of determination to establish working judiciary systems is one of the factors contributing to the anarchy."

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What -- can you tell us a little bit more about the state of the judiciary system at the time that you wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Different impressions from speaking with officials working in the framework of the judiciary, and [indiscernible] in Knin, led us to believe that there was an understaffing, that there was a lack of attention to bringing the proper working conditions to bear. The judiciary system would also, of course, require a well-run police force who would, on own initiative, initiate investigations and so on. Another example could be that instances -- I'll have to relate to my notes and reports to see the exact dates, where problems were brought to higher authorities, including General Cermak, did not receive the proper attention, in our mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You also --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lack of judiciary systems when it came to protecting civil property, of course, did not encourage people to come back. I do, in one of the reports, I remember, illustrate or give an example with a very simple case. I, off the top of my head, think that I say something like -- it is selected not because of the gravity of the crime but because it simple and straightforward, and that is just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me call up P47, Madam Registrar. Mr. Liborius, with the assistance of the usher, I'm putting on the screen a map of the town of Knin. You testified during the direct examination that on the 5th of August you saw a collection point for looted goods. And once we get that map on the screen, I'm going to ask you to circle the location in Knin where you saw the collection point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the right colour, again, for the Defence was blue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We'll have to find the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: P62, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meantime I'm happy to assist Mr. Misetic on developing the court issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's okay. We'll just wait for the map, Mr. Liborius. There we go. Mr. Liborius, off to the right is the UN Sector South headquarters, the UN camp, which is where you were on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with the assistance of the usher, with the blue marker, if could you circle the location where you saw the collection point for looted goods, please?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have it magnified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which portion would you like magnified?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the entrance to the UN Sector South barracks, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Meaning in the front of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If could you -- can I point or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, do you need a mouse. Is there a mouse?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a mouse. Doesn't work. Can we enlarge this section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the [indiscernible] part, bottom middle part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that help?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in more, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Madam Usher, could you assist Mr. Liborius with a blue pen. Or have you got it already? You can mark on the screen, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd ask -- I tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, I take, it Mr. Waespi. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be exhibit number D753.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D753 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could now have P825, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, this is the daily report for the 5th of August, and I'd ask you to go through it and see if you can find any reference to a collection point of -- for looted goods in your report. And I note that you are the sole author of the report.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we move down, please. And?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And there's a next page we can look at.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question was, if I could point to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not in your daily report for that day, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not be -- specifics would not be in every daily report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could now go to the daily report, the first daily report for the 6th of August, which I don't have a P number for yet, but it's 65 ter number 4005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to section 3 b there, again you're the author of this report. It says: "In and around Knin looting is widespread. The HV commanders seems to be disciplined, however, there are many reports to suggest that individual HV soldiers are not, beating civilians, robbing. There are strong indications of killings of ARSK soldiers after Knin had been taken. This morning the looting was still ongoing, a few houses were fire." If we could turn the page, please. And I note, if you can look at the header there it says this is written at 1547?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the next page, please. It says in section 5: "We and the rest of UN are still confined to barracks. UN Sector South commander now considers the UN forces to be held hostages by the HV. It is his strong belief that ethnic cleansing is being conducted by the HV." Now, first, when this report was written you still had not actually been able to go out in the town. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a few monitors who managed to negotiate their way through and had impressions from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, as of 1547 in this report, nobody got in the town. You said, "We and the rest of the UN are still confined to barracks." Do you see that? But there is a subsequent report that day where some of your monitors did manage to get into the town?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We could even look at that report --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- which is 65 ter 4007?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, perhaps we first deal with the previous one, 65 ter 4005. It is tendered by the Prosecution, if we already assign a P number to it, then we can admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 4005.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit number P826, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P826 is admitted into evidence. Now, I haven't got my list with me. Is 65 ter 4007 on that list as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It has been tendered by the Prosecution and we didn't get a P number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll get a P number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be exhibit number P827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P827 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Liborius, you see that same day now at 2150 both you and Mr. Bigland send a second report. Do you see that in the header?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to the next page, please. "SOO and several others went downtown just before dark without HV clearance and were allowed through the HV military police check-point by showing the ECMM go anywhere card." SOO refers to?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senior operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which would be Mr. Bigland?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "In town there were many soldiers, military police, and civilian police who were relaxed and friendly. If we waved at them they waved back and did not obstruct us." If we can go farther on down: "Some of the accommodation" -- sorry, "the office was visited and it was seemed to have been totally ransacked, but the only things missing were the TV, video, satellite system, and mobile phone. Some of the accommodation was visited and, again, the same story, ransacked, but all the personal belongings appear to be still there except for my Rolex Submariner." "There were several civilians on the street, and they appeared to be unafraid and fairly happy to stay. None asked for our assistance when we walked around and spoke to them." And then penultimate sentence is: "They are also siphoning fuel from any damage the vehicles which cannot be used, but apart from the TVs and electronic equipment the looting appears minimal. Even the office beer was left, so RC will have a quiet beer tonight." Mr. Liborius, is that an accurate state of affairs on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the impression of SOO, Richard Bigland for that particular trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In preparing the daily report, did you have any dispute with Mr. Bigland over his assessment of the state of events in Knin on the evening of the 6th?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a chance to discuss that with Mr. Bigland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you're the co-author of the report, and so if I may ask you how is it that your name is on the report and you sent it? Did you disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you yesterday that the production of the RC daily report would be going on throughout the day and that the person who then sent it and the input, Richard Bigland's input, was for his own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the last answer, sir, so let me ask it again. Did you sign off -- strike that. Did you review this report before it was sent to HQ ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll up to the top, please. First page. I'm just checking the time of transmission there. I would imagine that Mr. Bigland has sent it off. We did not sign off reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I asked you if you reviewed the report before it was sent off to HQ of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that shape it had there, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- why didn't you include in the report your finding from the day before of an HV collection point for lotted goods?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that, at that day, I was busy with a lot of other operational tasks. And with regard to your question, the previous report you showed, why it was not there, there would be different issues that would go into the daily reports. If you look at the first one, you would see that it was mainly how the status of the ECMM teams would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm actually more concerned with the fact that when the ECMM monitors finally got out on the evening of the 6th and could make an assessment based on their own observations, the conclusion was apart from TVs and electronic equipment, the looting appears minimal. And given that you have now shown us on the map that the collection point was right outside the UN compound, that would have been impossible for even Mr. Bigland to miss. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right outside, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if there were a HV collection point for looted goods located right outside the UN compound, based on what you said on direct testimony about 7th Guards Brigade showing off their loot, Mr. Bigland wouldn't have written that looting appears minimal, would he?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The loot there, at that point in time, was mainly in small private vehicles coming with exactly TV sets and all similar light issues -- light goods you could carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless it is written in the report, the looting was light, meaning that issue -- that the things you could easily just take with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually it says --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither looting as opposed to being heavy, means that heavy furniture, fixed appliances, heavier stuff, building materials and that stuff, would be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, it says that the looting appears minimal, not that the looting appears light. What, then, was located at the collection point? Describe the goods.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw TV sets, small electrical appliances, liquor bottles, cars being -- coming there. Things that could be easily transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And how long was that collection point there?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult to say. It -- a couple of days, you know, you get used to things like that in your immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, when you say a couple of days do you mean a couple of days more after the 6th?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So to the 8th?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about the 7th?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You talked about five -- the first wave of the looters were in groups of five to 15 uniformed HV soldiers and that you saw this, and my first question, sir, is -- let's talk about a specific event. This issue about you seeing the Diverzantia, which is, Madam Registrar, P807. And there, if we can scroll to number 3. First, sir, if you could review that and tell me whether that is something that you personally witnessed.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, yes, the Diverzantia I personally witnessed, and that is to my mind concerning mainly burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Okay. Burning. Let's stay on this topic, though.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Have we left looting or?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to it. You personally witnessed the skull as the insignia?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who was travelling with you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Marker-Hansen was travelling with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Eric Hendriks. I'm not a hundred per cent certain. Mr. Marker-Hansen was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You note in there that the Diverzantia belonged to the 7th Guards Brigade. Do you see that, the group belonging to 7 BDE?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did you determine that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the tactical signature of the vehicles and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says in the report that -- it said Diverzantia, the skull on their insignia?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever bother to check whether there is such a unit with such a patch in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You told us earlier in your direct testimony that you would do these patrols with a book that had the various badges of various different Croatian army formations. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the book, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you check in the book to see if there is any unit in the Croatian army that has a badge as with a skull as their insignia?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Diverzantia was noted by us when we encountered them. We had a lot of other business to attend to in those particular days. So it was not for us to look up in the larger recognition books which were not available to us. We had short books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you to learn that there was no such unit known as the Diverzantia with a skull on its insignia in 1995 in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written on the vehicle. So what surprises me -- I noted what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the last topic for today, sir, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we have to finish not one second later than 7.00. I don't know whether you have -- whether we could last --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I wish -- if you say I can deal can it in one minute, then it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not one minute, but I don't want to tell you I'm going to finish not more than one second, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then let's keep on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One point is that I'm unable to decipher the last name of the second name on this list, so if I can get some additional assistance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic has difficulty in reading your handwriting. Perhaps it could be returned to you right away, and if you perhaps write it in capitals so that Mr. Misetic can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if we could have a copy or see it at one point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Liborius, you're familiar already with the procedure, so I instruct you again, as I did the previous days, that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether it is the testimony you gave already, or the testimony still to be given. We adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I. We will continue to 6.00 in the afternoon. The parties will receive a schedule indicating what breaks we'll have. We have a slightly longer break for lunch-time. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
